No. The reply was as accurate as possible in the light of the information provided by Mr. Heakes, who had requested an inquiry respecting letters sent to his mother between December 1964 and November 1965 to three different addresses in the Toronto area. speechtext:

2. (1) Eastern Ontario Rural Development Study; This project covers the 11 eastern counties of Ontario and is primarily an economic evaluation of farm size, land capability, and mode of farming with the objective of establishing the requirements for the formation of viable farm units. The total cost of this project is estimated at $36,100, shared equally between federal ARDA and the province. (2) Drainage Assistance in eastern Ontario; There are 966,000 acres of land in the 11 counties of eastern Ontario which are poorly drained but which have a high capability for agriculture. A portion of this land is within Carleton county. During the next five years federal ARDA will provide one third of the funds for a $1,500,000 program to provide outlet drainage ditches. The balance of cost will be paid equally by the province and the municipalities involved. (3) Farm Pond Assistance Program; This provincial wide program is designed to increase farm productivity by supplementing farm water supply for livestock, spraying, and irrigation. During the next two years federal ARDA will contribute one quarter of the $700,000 to be expended; the provincial contribution will also be one quarter while the local contribution will be one half. The total federal provincial contribution may not exceed $500 for any one pond per 100 acres of land or fraction thereof. (4) The Canada Land Inventory; This $18,000,000 nation-wide survey will assess land capabilities for agriculture, forestry, recreation and wildlife. In addition, certain socio-economic factors will be evaluated. The work is probably more advanced in eastern Ontario than any other region of Canada. At the present time, the capabilities for agriculture and forestry and the present land use have been mapped in the eleven eastern counties. Work on the wildlife and recreation sectors of the inventory is presently underway in the same area. Federal ARDA will assume the entire cost of the inventory.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for York South, to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the labour dispute at Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec between the Shipping Federation of Canada and the international longshoremen's association, and its serious effects upon the economy of the country.
I would like an opportunity to make some remarks regarding the urgency of this matter.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order, please. I would invite the hon. member to submit remarks not about the urgency of the matter but about urgency of debate of the matter.

subtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS
subsubtopic: QUEBEC LONGSHOREMEN'S STRIKE-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall confine my remarks to the urgency of debate at this time. It is not necessary to point out to the house the widespread and harmful effects which a continuation of this labour dispute can have on the economy, the serious effect which it will have on the export of our goods and particularly grain shipments, which to a very large extent determines the deliveries which prairie farmers can make of their wheat.
The fact that there has been violence on the waterfront during the last 24 hours is something which I think causes great concern. We in this party do not for one moment condone that violence, but we suggest that the quickest way to bring an end to such violence is to find a speedy solution to the dispute.
We feel that a discussion in the house today will provide an opportunity for full discussion of the facts upon which the dispute is based. The house has not had an opportunity, other than by some fragmentary answers given by the Minister of Labour, to learn what is the real cause of the labour dispute and what are the points at issue. It seems only fair to both sides and to the public that these facts should be known and should be fully discussed in the hope that a solution can be reached.
I should like to point out that no other opportunity presents itself at this time to discuss this very important matter. We had hoped that the estimates of the Department

June 1, 1966

of Labour would have been before the house today; had that taken place it would not be necessary to raise this matter now. If the government decides to bring down the labour estimates this would obviate the necessity to proceed with this motion, but if there is no other opportunity it seems to us this matter ought to be discussed now.
As hon. members know, the labour estimates have been put at the end of the long list of departmental estimates announced by the Minister of Public Works last evening. It is unlikely that those estimates will be discussed before another ten days or two weeks. That is too long to wait before discussing a matter which is of such pressing importance and which could have such devastating consequences for the Canadian economy. For that reason we feel debate is urgent at this time in order that a full statement can be made by the Minister of Labour and hon. members may have an opportunity to debate this very important question.

speechtext: Shall vote No. 1 of the main estimates of the Department of Labour carry? This item appears on page 200 of the blue book of estimates, and was under consideration on Friday, May 27 last.

Mr. Chairman, I understand that the Minister of Labour said earlier today that he would be prepared to make a statement about the labour dispute which is now causing a good deal of dislocation in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec.
I wonder if the minister wants to make a statement at this time?

Mr. Chairman, my recollection of what I said yesterday, confirmed by a reference to Hansard, is that I would give consideration to the suggestion that was made, and that I might make a statement on motions today. I have considered that suggestion.
I intimated earlier this afternoon that the mediator has been working with the parties since nine o'clock this morning. Part of the difficulty, and I am sure that this is not through any lack of confidence on either side, is lack of communication in this particular field. The discussions taking place today are of the nature of an educational process, and communications between the parties are progressing within a more relaxed environment than previously, without the pressures that existed over the weekend. While these negotiations are progressing I do not think the minister ought to make a statement which might be taken out of context and might add to the difficulties that now exist.
My hon. friend sought to move a motion to adjourn the house. Nevertheless the estimates are before us. My hon. friend or any other member of the house may wish to comment, or make suggestions respecting this particular matter.

The minister's reticence at this time is rather difficult to understand in view of the fact that he has already made some statements, giving only part of the

DEBATES	June 1. 1966
story, with reference to the dispute now taking place within the port facilities of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec. I had hoped that the minister would take this opportunity of making a full and complete statement as to the basic causes of the strike.
Yesterday, when my friend and deskmate, the hon. member for York South asked the minister certain questions, the minister said that they would take too long to answer on orders of the day. Now that he has an excellent opportunity to give answers, he seems reluctant to do so.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
We want to know, Mr. Chairman, what is the major cause of this strike? The minister in his statement to the house on Monday last, May 30-

I hesitate to interrupt the hon. gentleman. Respecting the telegram that the hon. member questioned me about yesterday, may I point out that I did receive one telegram the day before yesterday. I think that the telegram the hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam received illustrates the point I have just tried to make. Some of the persons interested in this matter have failed to appreciate suggestions which have been made to them. In that connection I think it might help if I read a wire that went off this morning, for use by the mediator, if helpful. That wire is to Mr. Tremblay to whom the hon. member referred yesterday. Mr. Tremblay is the Atlantic coast district vice president of the ILA. My wire reads:
Retel 31 May during the further discussions taking place today I have asked that your representations be given consideration regarding the older longshoremen who would be affected by reduction of gangs with a view to devising arrangements that would accommodate them. Would also say that my statement in the House of Commons was subjected to observations and inferences that were unwarranted and out of context. There was no prejudicial reflection on my part on the position of your organization.
Because of that communication, and others, I feel that a statement by me as minister at this time would not be opportune or advisable.

Mr. Chairman, I must respectfully differ with the minister. It seems to me that a statement would be very much in order, particularly if it were to clarify some of the statements which he made on Monday, which statements in my opinion were highly inaccurate.
June 1, 1966

It is not a matter of being out of context. The first telegram dated May 30, which the minister received from the Gerard Tremblay pointed out to the minister that the main obstacle to the settlement of the longshoremen's strike lay in the fact that the shipping federation insisted on reducing gangs, and only guaranteeing job security to 85 per cent of the workers. This meant that 15 per cent of the workers would be laid off.
When I asked the minister about that, what was the minister's reply? At page 5675 of Hansard he said this:
The shipping federation offers job security for all the people who had worked for more than a given period of last year; in fact they offered job security for all those who had worked, I think, for more than 15 or 16 weeks. That was put forward for consideration. This is where the figure of 85 per cent comes in. I am advised that the other 15 per cent or less comprises the casual groups such as the taxi drivers, students and those who work for a limited period each year.
That was the minister's statement. The fact is, as was pointed out in the telegram sent to the minister by Mr. Gerard Tremblay, that these are not casual workers, taxi drivers and students; they are longshoremen who, because they have not yet reached the age of 65, are not old enough to receive a pension. But they are too old to work the entire shipping season. They do not work part of the time on the docks and part of the time at something else. They work part time on the docks because they do not have the physical strength and stamina to work full time. They work part of the day and go home for a rest. Remember, this is exacting, physical labour. The minister gave the house and the country the impression that these men-the regular longshoremen-would not be kicked out and that this proposed lay-off of 15 per cent would apply only to casual workers such as taxi drivers and students.
The union is contending that these older men who are not able to work the whole shipping season should not be thrown into the discard. It is not only a matter of losing a job. If an older worker who yet has several years to go before retirement, is thrown out at this time, he will not be eligible for a pension at the age of 65; he will lose all the benefits and pension rights he has built up for 20 or 30 years. This is a fundamental point. The rest of the longshoremen are fighting a battle, not for themselves but for this 15 per cent of the older workers who cannot work full time and who would not only be out of a job but completely without security at the 23033-3701
Supply

Labour
age of 65, should they be callously discarded now by the shipping federation.
Surely the Minister of Labour must be aware that a couple of years ago his predecessor appointed Judge Lippe as a commissioner of inquiry to look into the matters which were disturbing the smooth operation of port facilities, particularly in Montreal. In the course of this inquiry Judge Lippe recognized the existence of this problem involving the older workers. He recognized that where such heavy physical labour is demanded the retirement age ought to be lower -probably 60 years-but that in the meantime some agreement for the partial retirement of these men in the 60-65 age group should be brought about.
Had the government acted on this recommendation which, I understand, Judge Lippe made, the problem would not now have arisen. But it exists, and instead of recognizing it and trying to get the shipping federation to accept a solution, the minister informs the house that all is well-that there is really no problem and that the 15 per cent who are to be thrown out of work are students, taxi drivers and people who are not really longshoremen at all. Well, the information I have is that they are longshoremen-men who have spent the best part of their lives working on the docks and who are entitled to some job security and protection.
When I asked the minister whether the Freedman principle ought not to apply, the minister answered, as reported on page 5676 of Hansard:
-even Mr. Justice Freedman did not suggest that casual employees should be looked after in the way suggested in the telegram.
My understanding of the Freedman proposal was that where technological change makes it desirable to reduce the work force, this should be a matter for negotiation and that some of the benefits of technological change should be passed on to the workers and used to provide retirement benefits for those thrown out of work by automation. Mr. Speaker, if ever there was an example of a need to apply the Freedman formula, surely it is in this instance.
The other question which has not been clarified by the minister has to do with wages. I asked the minister a question about this on Monday last, in reply to which he said, as reported on page 5675:
As I have said, very substantial increases-some say fantastic increases, I would suggest-in pay were offered. In return for these, the shipping federation has suggested, and I think properly, that they

June 1, 1966
Supply-Labour
might expect increased productivity during the second year of the agreement.
I think the house has a right to know the extent of these so-called fantastic increases.
My hon. friend from York South (Mr. Lewis) tried to find this out. He asked the minister yesterday whether the offer which was submitted to the longshoremen was a figure submitted by the minister as a bargaining basis or whether it was a figure which had been accepted by the shipping federation and which the hon. gentleman had been authorized to offer to the longshoremen. It was at this point that the minister said it would take too long to give an answer on the orders of the day.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
They are quite within their rights in suggesting, whatever wage increase is offered to them, that before they agree to any reduction in the work gangs they have a right to some assurance that this 15 per cent of the workers who are to be displaced will be given proper job protection and proper security in their old age.
My reason for raising this matter today is that I think that the longshoremen have a right to have their case presented fairly and properly. I do not suggest that I can present it fairly and properly. I have not taken part in the negotiations. I do not know what wage increases have been offered to them. All I have seen is an exchange of telegrams-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Does the hon. member not think that an experienced counsel in the field of labour relations, who has been with this matter for several weeks, is in a better position to explain this situation to his clients with the assistance of the mediator, rather than a discussion in this house?

Mr. Chairman, the experienced counsel is not in this house. What I am seeking to do is to point out that the only information that has been given to the house regarding this labour dispute has come from the minister, and his statement of Monday last sounded like a press release from the shipping federation.
If the minister wants to pose as the spokesman for the employers, then let him get into a department where he will be such a spokesman for the employers, and not stay in the

labour department where he is supposed to be unbiased and impartial. I am saying that the longshoremen have a right to have their case presented fairly. It has not been presented fairly by the minister, and that has been shown by the telegrams exchanged between himself and Mr. Gerard Tremblay.
The minister has not given the house the facts. It is from the statements of the minister that the people will gather their impression as to the reason for this labour dispute. The minister has not told the house all the facts with reference to the 15 per cent of the men who are to be thrown out of jobs. He has not told the house and the country what sort of wage offer has been made, and whether it has been made by the employers or merely made by him as a basis for negotiations.
In the telegram which the minister received from Mr. Tremblay, the latter stated that the longshoremen have not yet received a written reply to the offer they submitted to the shipping federation. That is why we want to know whether this wage offer is a definite offer, made in writing, to which the shipping federation is committed, or are these merely figures which the minister is using in the process of negotiation? Until we have this kind of information we do not know what is the real cause of the dispute.
The people of Canada are naturally concerned about this strike. It is doing great harm to our export trade. The Minister of Finance has already told us that some 25 million bushels of grain which should be shipped are held up. The public is going to become increasingly annoyed at the delay in shipping.
As a member of the house I am anxious to know where the responsibility lies. Does it lie with the men? Are the men being unreasonable in their demands? Are they asking too much? Or, does the responsibility lie with the shipping federation? Is it trying to use this present situation as an excuse for throwing 15 per cent of its employees out of jobs merely because those employees have become older and less able to work? Is it trying to use this situation to get rid of employees to whom it will have to pay a pension in a few years? Is it trying to use this situation as a means of cutting down overhead and avoiding obligations with reference to some of its workers who have been working for it for over a quarter of a century?
We want to know. The country has a right to know. The whole issue has been befogged
June 1. 1966

and beclouded by the statements of the minister. Today the minister is very reticent, but he was not so reticent on Monday when he was presenting the employers' side of the case. There is no reason why he should be so reticent today.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Does the hon. member think he is contributing to the settlement of this strike by questioning the impartiality of the Minister of Labour?
Hear, hear.
The same old cry.
Mr. Chairman, this is the first time I ever knew that statements of ministers have become sacrosanct.
You are questioning the impartiality.

I am saying that any person who will read the minister's statement of last Monday, which I put on the record, will recognize whether or not the minister has been partial in this matter. The minister makes the statement that a proposed increase is fantastic, and then refuses to tell the house whether or not this was an actual increase offered by the management.
A minister who describes 15 per cent of the people who are being laid off, not as longshoremen but as taxi drivers and students, without having checked the records in the central bureau of the St. Lawrence river ports, and a minister who quotes figures on the basis of the information given to him by the shipping federation, certainly in my opinion is not acting in an impartial manner.
I am not raising this in order to make a settlement more difficult. I am raising it because I do not want the Canadian people to be under any misapprehension as to the cause of this strike. If there is information we have not got, then let the minister give it to us. But I am saying that in so far as the limited information I have, which is merely in the telegrams that have been exchanged between the vice president of the I.L.A. and the minister, it would indicate that the basic problem has to do with the reduction of work gangs, that the people being displaced are in a great many cases long service longshoremen, and that the only reason they are able
Supply-Labour
to work for only part of the shipping season is because of their age and infirmity.
And I say that if those facts are correct, the longshoremen are fully justified in saying that those men ought to have some consideration, and that merely paying the younger and able bodied workers a little more money does not give the shipping federation the right to toss the old men out on to the scrap heap.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I just want to say that this dispute is only one of many that are on the horizon. The seaway employees, disputes in Air Canada and the C.B.C. are only the ones that have come under federal jurisdiction, but there is hardly a province of Canada in which there are not labour negotiations proceeding, and threatened strikes. I am sorry that in many cases where they come under his jurisdiction the results of these labour disputes will be placed on the doorstep of the Minister of Labour.
For over two years we in this party have been trying to warn the government that these labour disputes will become more common and more violent unless the government faces up to two problems. First there is the steady increase in the cost of living, and every increase in the cost of living is inevitably followed by a demand for increased wages. That is only natural. Unless the government is prepared to bring down some program that will meet the difficulty of the rising cost of living, they can expect more labour disputes and not less.
The other problem which we have pointed out to them is that automation is going to be an increasing factor in causing economic dislocation. The investigation by Mr. Justice Freedman laid down the principle and that principle now has to be worked out in terms of practical legislation. The government now at long last is getting around to the setting up of a department of manpower, and talking about re-training. But three valuable years have been wasted. Little or nothing has been done to set the stage for the problems of automation and the solutions which must be found to those problems.
Last Friday, at page 5632 of Hansard, the minister made what I thought was a most amazing proposal. He said:
I have not been in this office long enough to be able to say whether the solution lies in the establishment of arbitration or of labour courts, such as those that have been set up in Australia and other countries of the world. The answer may lie in that kind of action because, while they have had divided success, on the whole they have been successful.

June 1, 1966
Supply-Labour
I throw that idea out as something that merits the serious consideration of all members of this house and of all Canadians.
Well, Mr. Chairman, surely this is a policy of despair when a government, which says it cannot do anything about the rising cost of living, is prepared to do something when workers demand increased wages to meet the rising cost of living. What is proposed? It proposes that it may set up courts for compulsory arbitration so that it may say to the worker: "Somebody other than you will determine the price of your labour." The government is not prepared to determine the price that the Steel Company of Canada, Limited, will get for steel or that General Motors Corporation will get for a car, or that Canada Packers Limited will get for a pound of bacon; but the government is prepared to consider setting up an authority which will determine what price the worker will be paid for his sweat and his toil.
Surely the government does not think they can get away with that. The setting up of the kind of court which the minister has proposed is simply an indication-
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.

Are you suggesting that I proposed such a thing? Did I not also ask the advice of the house on the question of some other possible solution? Will the hon. member please read another passage which will show that the remarks he quoted were taken out of context. I refer to the passage at page 5636 of Hansard, where the very item to which he is referring was raised in a question by the hon. member for Middlesex West. I think one of the difficulties in respect of taking statements out of context is that it gives rise to trouble. I would appreciate it if the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would read the question and answer at page 5636 of Hansard.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I would be very glad to read the question, but I should like to point out to the minister that in addition to the statements which he made in the house last Friday, he has been making statements outside the house along this line. I listened to one of them myself when he appeared on television. The minister may say that he is not making this as a firm proposal, but I certainly would suggest to him in all kindness that he cannot blame the public if they gain the impression that he is trying to condition public thinking to the introduction

of such a policy. The general feeling of many of us is-
Mr. Chairman, is the hon. member not going to read the passage?

Surely. I was going to say to the minister that I get the impression that he is flying a kite to see what public reaction will be to compulsory arbitration.
The minister at page 5636 of Hansard was asked a question by Mr. Thomas (Middlesex West), and the question is:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question while his mind is still on the point. Has consideration been given by his department to the use of compulsory arbitration as a means of settling disputes, rather than resorting to strike action, as has been the case for many years?
Then the minister said:
I am going to suggest that I take note of questions and deal with them perhaps at the end of the period. However, I think this particular question merits a special answer and I would be glad to give one.
Very serious consideration has been given to this matter by the department and by experienced departmental officials over a period of several years. As a member of cabinet I know something of the difficulties that we have had in trying to work out and find an acceptable formula. If you really believe, as I happen to, in the importance and the significance of collective bargaining, which enables management and labour to sit down on opposite sides of the table and unburden their hearts and take strong positions if necessary, it is difficult to say in all cases compulsory arbitration would be necessary, or advisable.
I ask the minister to look at that.
Please read the next paragraph.
The minister said that it would be difficult to say in all cases compulsory arbitration would be necessary or advisable. Is he saying that in some cases it would be necessary?
Just read the next paragraph please, and do not stop in the middle of the excerpt.

I will read the next paragraph to the minister. It would be much better for him to make a speech, but if he wants me to make it for him, fine.
On the other hand, I think-and I am speaking only for myself, certainly not for the government, nor do I even express the consensus of my department-there are many cases where the national interest is at stake. I can think of safety and security in the air line industry, for instance, where weather services have to be maintained. Then there is the movement of passengers and freight in many cases on our railroads. It is just as Important perhaps,
June 1, 1966

In my view, to have compulsory arbitration in these fields as in certain aspects of civil service activities, as proposed in the legislation that is now before this house.
The minister certainly has not helped anything by asking me to read. The fact that he now enumerates some of the economic activities in which he would support compulsory arbitration-
Would you read the next paragraph please.

Before I go on to read the other paragraph which the minister wants read, may I point out that since he already has dealt with the handling of freight and the operation of the railways, I suppose the loading of ships comes in much the same category. Do I take it that he is now going to include the longshoremen among the categories which should come under compulsory arbitration? I will read the last paragraph:
I cannot give the hon. member a definite answer, but I can assure him-and this is why I made the appeal earlier today-that any constructive suggestions, which any member of this house or any other person may have to make as to how we might solve this extremely difficult question, when our national interests and economy are at stake, would be very welcome.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to be unkind to the minister, but I want to say that I am sure if the Liberal government had gone to the country last November and said to the people, "As soon as we assume office we will generally advertise, asking anyone who has any idea about how to run this country to please submit it and it will be received, but in the meantime we have not the remotest idea what we are going to do about this matter," they would never have been elected. I am sure that if they had said, "As soon as we get into office we will open a special mailbox to receive-"

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. gentleman another question. Is he suggesting that a minister of the crown should not invite the views and opinions of members of this house. I thought that was one reason why we were having a debate this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to the minister's asking for suggestions. As a matter of fact, I will make some in a moment. What we are saying is that surely there ought to be some leadership given by this government. Surely a government that asked the people of Canada to elect
Supply-Labour
it to office should give some leadership. Surely a party that has talked about 60 days of decision should not be now saying: We do not know what to do about rising prices, automation and labour discords such as have occurred as a result of our inaction and inertia. Surely a government after dawdling for three years, doing nothing about rising living costs, and doing nothing about bringing in legislation to resolve the problems created by automation and technological change ought to give us something better than a statement by a minister to the effect that as soon as the people tell them what they should do they will do something.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his allotted time has expired.
Sone hon. Members: Carry on.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party; Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is it agreed that the hon. member should be allowed to continue his speech?
Agreed.
Mr. Chairman, I shall take only a few more minutes, but I might say that at least one quarter of my time has been spent in reading the minister's speech for him, at his request.
Is that not a penalty you must pay when you read excerpts from Hansard?

The minister has spoken about suggestions that might be made. Let me inform him that he did not have to wait until now for suggestions. We on this side of the house have been making suggestions to the government for the past three years, pointing out that this country, along with the rest of the western world, has now embarked upon a great scientific revolution, and that technological change is taking place altering our whole way of life, and will alter it even more in the decades that lie ahead.
This country must adapt itself to completely changed conditions and entirely different situations. The old techniques will not suffice, and it will not do for the government to sit with its eyes shut to a steadily increasing cost of living, and do nothing. The government has done nothing about automation in the past three years but now comes to us and says it is in a mess because workers want more wages because it costs more to buy groceries in the stores. The government has said that workers are out on strike because

June 1, 1966
Supply-Labour
some employers want to throw 15 per cent of their employees on the scrap heap, but that if the people have any suggestions, they would like to hear them. Surely that is not good government.
This government has known for three years that these problems existed, but they have swept them under the rug and turned a blind eye to other major economic problems which face this country. The government is now wallowing in a mess, yet the very best it can say is: We would be glad to have some suggestions from the opposition.
Let me conclude by returning to my original point. I hope the minister will now make a statement clarifying the situation with reference to the strike taking place at the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec, and that he will tell us exactly what the employers have offered in writing, and what the employees are demanding. I hope he will tell us what steps the government is taking to try to resolve the difference that may exist between the positions taken by the two disputants. If the minister can give us that kind of information we will then be in a better position to assess where responsibility lies and decide what steps must be taken to reach a solution.

Mr. Chairman, I think there will be general agreement with the views expressed by the hon. member who preceded me, that there has been gross delay and inactivity on the part of this government. The strike has gone on now for several weeks, since May 9 or 10, and regularly we have been led to believe that everything was being done by the government that could be done to bring about a solution to this strike, which is becoming more serious with the passing days.
Let me quote the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce in answer to a question posed by the hon. member for Lisgar. The minister is reported at page 5743 of Hansard for May 31 as follows:
-I can say the matter is of the very greatest concern to the Canadian Wheat Board.
The situation is of concern to the farmers in the province of Quebec who need feed to operate their dairy farms. This is something that concerns law and order in every part of Canada, particularly when one realizes that in order to divert a new waterfront eruption 300 policemen are on duty, and that in spite of this fact violence has already taken place. The only answer we can get from the government takes the form of a suggestion that
[Ur. Douglas.]
nothing is being done about it, but ultimately it will disappear. That is a strange proposition.
Perhaps some explanation can be found in the fact that after this government has been in office for three years individuals like the president of the professional association of millers of Quebec do not even realize that there has been a change of government. This fact indicates the tremendous impact that has been made by the present government.
Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question? Does he not regard that as a compliment to him?

It certainly does not indicate a compliment as far as the government of Canada today is concerned. The president of that association of millers sent me a telegram in which he said:
Have just heard on radio that you stated that we could pick up the feed grain with trucks at the port elevators. What about the stevedores who will not allow the trucks to get to the elevators and also will not allow non-striking port employees to get to their work. This is what is happening at the elevators in Quebec. For the last time, accept your responsibilities before it is too late.
He did not even know that the Minister of Labour was around or that this government was in office, because he put the blame on us. What is the government doing about this situation? Are they waiting and hoping, and like Barkis, willin'? While the government waits, making the kind of equivocal statements to which reference has been made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, things are becoming worse and worse.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
All of us have heard the old legend about Rome burning and Nero fiddling. One has only to think of the activities of this government to realize that this example does not begin to describe the indolence, inactivity and inaction of this government. I listened with interest to what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam said as to what could be done. He was in office in the province of Saskatchewan. That was of course before there was any alliance with any great labour unions. But I recall that there were strikes when the C.C.F., the parent body of the N.D.P., was in office. I remember even in 1953 that the provincial transportation system was tied up because of a strike.
As I listened to the hon. member-and this seems to be a characteristic of that group as they wrap about themselves the mantle of perfection-I recalled something of the cost of
June 1, 1966

living within the province of Saskatchewan. After all, action on price fixing is a matter for the provinces, except in an emergency, and then only in circumstances permitted under the War Measures Act. As the hon. member spoke a moment ago as to action that might be taken, I recalled so well that in 1946, I think it was, the government of Saskatchewan, the socialist government of Saskatchewan, passed legislation that all prices in Saskatchewan had to be approved, that increases in prices that could not be justified could result in action being taken. I have said before that the legislation was never brought in, because it had to be proclaimed and they never proclaimed it. I have often mentioned the fact that if they had brought it in there would have been only three classes of persons in Saskatchewan: those in jail, others waiting to get in, and the rest waiting to be tried. They did not bring it in, but they have the solutions now. I would like to know what those solutions are.
They talk of the results of automation, and certainly automation is one of the most tremendous challenges throughout the free world. But how are you going to meet it? Not by the kind of generalizations that were mentioned today; not by rising and simply saying, "We have in our minds what could be done"; not by an alliance with great labour unions. Indeed, alliances of that kind are now being frowned upon in the United States. Only a few days ago Mr. George Meany, head of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., enunciated the principle of the danger of a great union's being allied with a political party. That union of his was part and parcel of the Democratic party; it won a couple of elections as a result. But the other day he expressed grave fears as to whether there should be any continuance of that alliance. Indeed, I interpreted his remarks to mean that no labour union of any importance should again find itself in a position of being allied with a political party: for after all, all of us have done our part for labour; none of us has any monopoly.
I look at my hon. friends opposite, and they give the impression as they speak that only they have any affection for labour. Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to review the years and go back over history, but the very foundation of trade unionism was under Macdonald in the face of great trouble, difficulties and opposition; and through the years no political party has had a monopoly of the desire that labour should receive its fair consideration. That has been the history of
Supply-Labour
this matter. But when I listen day after day to the unctuous pronouncements of my hon. friends to the left, I ask myself, "Do they mean it? Are they as sincere as they appear? Has sincerity become something that only they possess in this regard?" I give my hon. friends the opportunity of clarifying this, and I am sure they will; they are great debaters.
I have heard these things over and over again, sir, and this afternoon I feel compelled to say a word in this regard. They often lead us to believe that there is something wrong with parliament, and that if only we had a socialist government things would be so different. We had a socialist government in Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Bur-naby-Coquitlam was the premier of that province, and with distinction. They had such bitterness in the legislature of Saskatchewan that the leader of the opposition sued the premier of Saskatchewan and they went through to the Supreme Court of Canada. Of course, that is in the past.
Oh, oh.

I am simply pointing out that I remember so well the debates in Saskatchewan, and the legislature then was not always that peaceful, namby-pamby kind of institution which they today would indicate the rest of us should make the House of Commons. They are only human beings and they are following the usual ways of human beings. I thought I ought to point this out because, Mr. Chairman, week after week they rise, they speak, and sometimes as I listen to them I think of the words of Agrippa, "Almost thou persuadest me..." It might be that I could be persuaded if I had not had the experience in Saskatchewan.
However, I know they will understand that I was just provoked into this and thought I should make a few references to this matter, because we have listened now for three years to this kind of thing. While I have every regard for the contribution that was made by the socialist government of Saskatchewan in social welfare, I am not unmindful of the fact that our province went back economically and in population during the days of socialism.
Mr. Chairman, could I ask the Leader of the Opposition a question?
Certainly.

Could I ask the Leader of the Opposition if it is possible for him to lower

Supply-Labour
his halo a little bit, and will Diefenbaker the almighty now tell the government and this house how to handle the situation in Montreal, with which we are most concerned?
Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman's halo choked him long ago.
Hear, hear.
Will you now advise the house how to handle the problem?

I am asking the government now to give us some idea of what they have in mind.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I was quite surprised to find the Minister of Labour coming out so strongly in favour of compulsory arbitration. He asked the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam to read on. As he did this I was reminded of Right Hon. Mackenzie King. You could never catch him: Of course he was the hon. member for Prince Albert. If you quoted anything that he had said, he would tell you "Read on". Sooner of later you could be absolutely sure to find the very reverse of what he had said earlier. Apparently the Minister of Labour is also of that school; he says "Read on".

Mr. Chairman, may I put a question to the right hon. gentleman? Is it not a fact that he said on more than one occasion he was a great admirer of prime minister King as a political tactician in the house? Does the same compliment apply to the Minister of Labour?

All I can say is that whatever were his powers of extraterrestrial communication, often he came up with the right answer. I must say that the Minister of Transport also possesses ability in that direction. I think the Minister of Labour might consult him and find that answers will be forthcoming, such as they may be.
I wish to ask the minister whether or not the views expressed in the several telegrams that have been sent by Gerard Tremblay are in fact borne out by the facts? I have received a telegram which I will read to you and I will ask the minister to give us his answer to this. It says:
We disagree with claim that shipping federation has offered to guarantee employment for all regular longshoremen-
Will the minister say whether regular longshoremen will be guaranteed employment?
[Mr. Winch.3
Will they be guaranteed their pension rights? It goes on to say:
It is not true that all longshoremen who work 750 hours or less in navigation season are casual employees. Many of them are longshoremen who are too young to die or to receive a pension at age 65 and too old to work.
Will the minister clarify this? Will he place facts before the house and the country? It goes on to say:
Recommendations of Judge Lippe when he was commissioner in inquiry ordered by your predecessor Hon. MacEachen concerning St. Lawrence river and maritime ports re some sort of partial retirement prior to pension that can only be obtained at age 65. Urge you to examine statistics available from central records bureau for St. Lawrence river ports . . . Regret that you qualify employer's offer as fantastic.
That was the wage offer.
Will the minister say what this "fantastic" offer was? Up to the present time all we know about it is the generalization. For weeks on end there has been a cavalier disregard by this government. They say "All will be well. We cannot act now because something will interfere with this action." My hon. colleague, the former minister of labour, asked the following question which appears at page 5743 of Hansard:
I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister. In view of the difficulties that are now being experienced... will the Prime Minister call the parties involved to Ottawa, to bring them into a different atmosphere so they may proceed to a settlement through the collective bargaining arrangement, under the chairmanship of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Marchand), who has a great deal of experience in this type of work?
This is amazing. Mr. Marchand-and I use his name only because of the reference I intend to make rather than referring to his constituency-is a man with wide experience in labour matters. Why is he not brought into this? The Minister of Industry has not had much experience in this field. The hon. member for Verdun-I am sure has had experience. But what about the Minister of National Health and Welfare? He should be in on this as he is a man of great experience.
Hear, hear.

I am always willing to speak of the qualities of any minister opposite, and I wonder why he was not used. It would have been a great opportunity to use his experience. What they did is to get only the Minister of Industry, because he comes from Montreal, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour, the hon. member for Verdun. Why did they not bring in someone with experience? I am glad to
June 1, 1966

hear the applause that greeted the mention of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It indicates there is agreement over there that he should do something. Why was he not called in? Why did they simply bring together the lame and the blind to deal with this problem? This is something I would like to know.
The Prime Minister said:
Mr. Speaker, everything that can be done is being done to bring this strike to an end. The Minister of Labour is in touch with the situation, as my hon. friend knows, and if and when the time comes that the minister who is dealing with the matter feels the intervention of the Prime Minister would be helpful, naturally he will let me know.
How long must the shipping transportation of Canada be held up before the government believes that some action should be taken?
They want 60 days for decision.

I said to the Prime
Minister that in view of the request which the Prime Minister received from the Montreal port council, the council stated that any further delay in settlement would be "catastrophic". Think of the tremendous loss each day. The Wheat Board is piling up wheat which cannot be shipped. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says it is a very trying and difficult situation, and yet there is nonchalance and an easy-going uncertainty on the part of the government. They are in a rut. After all, there was always support in the house from some hon. gentleman to the left. Why has some action not been taken?
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The hon. gentleman for Burnaby-Coquitlam said there would be an increasing number of strikes unless action is taken. What does this mean? He said that one of the reasons is the tremendously high cost of living, which goes up continually. There has been no action, nothing but wait and hope. They expect charity to come to their rescue. If ever there was an example of the inertia of a government, this is one. I repeat that three weeks, 21 or 22 days, have passed and the answer is: We are thinking about it. While the wheels of commerce cease to turn, the government of Canada refuses to take any action whatever. Surely if ever there was a problem that should be dealt with in part by the proposed department of manpower, this is one. What about the great Mr. Kent? You recall his name. He is the head of the war on poverty. We have not heard of him, but he ought to be in on this problem.

Again, I say why has not the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the minister of manpower to be, been called upon? If the statements made in the telegram from the workers, from Gerard Tremblay, are correct, then the workers have some justification for what they are doing. Before any of us can prescribe we have to know the facts. I now ask the minister to absolve himself from his vow of silence, and if he can get any help from the President of the Privy Council I will not object to hearing from him. He comes from Montreal-and that is the No. 1 qualification because no one can get into these discussions unless he comes from Montreal. This is what barred the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: What about the Minister without Portfolio; he is from Montreal?

Well, he has other responsibilities. Let us hear from the minister, and then I will have something further to say. In all seriousness, sir, can you not see yourselves if you were sitting over here, and we were in the government? The hon. member for Ontario, and I never said this about him before, was a minister of labour who understood matters and got things done. But if a strike continued even for a few days, the virulence of the attack that was launched on uj was something to behold.
I do not say that the present minister is not acquainted with the problems of labour. As a corporation man throughout the years he dealt with labour. He has about him a kindliness that should certainly have results if given an opportunity to operate. Before having anything further to say on this matter, I ask the minister to dispel this aura of silence that seems to have gripped the government with regard to this problem, and let us know the facts.
This is not something like mounted police records that can be spread about, as in the Vachon case. They are pretty good at that-spreading about slander, and destroying. This is a practical thing. I hope the minister will be prepared now to place the house in possession of the facts, and will be able to do that which will be almost impossible: to explain how the government of which he is a member has sat, considered, examined and done nothing effective for so long.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I have to admit, Mr. Chairman, it is difficult to follow the Leader

June 1, 1866
Supply-Labour
of the Opposition. I enjoyed his speech because I realized that the greater part of it was delivered with tongue in cheek.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I particularly appreciated his remarks, which I thought were so accurate, not pertaining to the strike but pertaining rather to the sanctimonious attitude of the socialist party which sits in this house. As a labour man-and I consider myself a labour man-I do not apologize to the Leader of the Opposition for having participated in the discussion on the week end. I can recall in 1942 supplementing my income when I was in university by working as a longshoreman on the Montreal waterfront. I became aware of many of the problems that labour is discussing in 1966 because they existed even then in 1942 and 1943. I sympathize with labour on many of the aspects of this situation.
As a labour man I was somewhat appalled at the efforts of the leader of the New Democratic Party earlier in the day when, under the guise of being concerned for labour, he callously rose in this house to demand an emergency debate on the longshoremen's strike, knowing full well, or at least he should have known as a labour representative, that a debate confined to that particular strike could have gone a long way toward jeopardizing, indeed neutralizing, much of the progress that had been made over the week end. There has been progress made today in Montreal.
Will you report on that progress?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
More and more, I get a little nauseated at the sanctimonious attitude adopted by the socialists in so far as labour is concerned. I think it is time they started showing some responsibility in the house and stopped jeopardizing the cause of labour under the guise of being the spokesmen for labour in the House of Commons. Knowing most members of the house as I do, I find no shortage of spokesmen for labour in our party or in the ranks of the official opposition.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
What this situation needs is more frankness and blunt talk, and less hypocrisy. I know that the minister will be speaking later in this debate, and I will leave it to his good judgment to divulge to the house what he

thinks should be divulged of the in camera sessions of Friday, Saturday morning, all day Sunday and Monday morning.
I should like to express my views as to some of the problems preventing the settlement of this costly strike on the waterfront. It is not a question any more of dollars and cents. It is no longer a question of how much management should pay or how much labour wants. The leader of the New Democratic Party was accurate in his assessment that we are now entering a new phase of management and labour relations. This country, now an industrial nation, can no longer afford the luxury of having segments of society pulling against each other, if we are to continue prospering.
The problems and aspirations of management must be the problems and aspirations of labour, and vice versa. Judge Freedman recognized this in his historic document. Similar to the document drawn a decade ago by Judge Rand, I believe the one drawn by Judge Freedman will, in time, be incorporated into the dictionary of labour terms. [DOT]
In all fairness to the present Minister of Labour, he was one of the first both inside and outside this house to endorse, espouse and advance the philosophy of Judge Freedman. Only last month in a speech in Vancouver, not to labour but to manufacturers, he warned the manufacturers association of the moral obligations they had to the people working for them, a moral obligation put on paper by Judge Freedman, a moral obligation which management must realize more and more.
Underlying this strike, Mr. Chairman, is the concept of the moral obligation management has to longshoremen who suffer from arthritis, heart attacks, fractured limbs, colds, exposure to the elements, and from 10, 15 or 20 years on the waterfront loading and unloading ships under the crudest of circumstances. Management has a responsibility to these people. The Minister of Labour made that abundantly clear to both parties in this dispute.
Many people in my constituency are longshoremen. Stripped of the propaganda of what is sometimes an unfriendly press, stripped of the gangster elements that periodically infiltrate the waterfronts around the world, the average longshoreman emerges, in the ports of Montreal, Trois-Rivieres and Quebec as an average and decent man, wanting no more for himself and his family than I, or you, Mr. Chairman, or any other
June 1, 1966

Canadian would want. My sympathies lie with the longshoreman and I do not hesitate
to say so.
We must expect management to accept the philosophy of the Freedman report, just as we must expect management of a railway, when a line is abandoned, to accept its legal and moral obligations to all those who lived in the towns or villages, whose lives have been disrupted by the unilateral decision of the railway.
On the other hand, labour must realize its responsibilities to management, if there is to be teamwork. We must develop and encourage in Canada co-operation between management and labour, so that if management recognizes its responsibilities under the Freedman report, labour must realize that if this country is to maintain its competitive position in the markets of the world, it cannot resist technological changes, new inventions, or new ways and means of increasing productivity per manpower hour.
This fundamentally is the issue. In all fairness to management, to the shipping federation, and to labour, this is a new concept which has been introduced into the scheme of things for the first time. Perhaps the parties have been tardy; but after all, free bargaining between management and labour is going on. Perhaps I am revealing secrets out of school but, under persuasion by the Minister of Labour, management has accepted responsibility to the people dislodged by automation, and labour has accepted its responsibility to co-operate in ways and means that will increase productivity, in the final analysis making our products exportable and not subject to inefficiency and high shipping costs.
It might asked, why, if both sides have accepted such principles, this strike has not been settled? I submit it is because this is the first time that such a concept has been introduced in this area of labour relations. There are differences of opinion between management and labour as to what the moral obligations on either side are. Those moral obligations have not been set out before in written form. It is only logical and normal, therefore, when you are dealing with six locals, and with a multiplicity of shipping concerns, that there should be differences of opinion.
Labour in the Montreal area is represented by a very efficient and responsible legal adviser, who has the respect of the minister, as well as of management. It is significant that the only point of difference at the moment
Supply-Labour
between the parties is not a question of wages, salaries, or costs per hour, but what are the moral obligations of the parties, and to whom those apply.
I do not feel that anyone can evaluate moral responsibility toward longshoremen in terms of the number of hours that have to be worked in one year. I think it is necessary to go into the histories of people. In case any hon. member asks for information. I might point out that labour had tentatively consented, provided everything else meets with their approval, to the appointment of a conciliator whose role it would be to see whether work gangs could be reduced moderately-not immediately but, say, in one year from now.
Labour has said in return: If we accept such a proposition, which would mean that possibly 200 or 300 men in total would be out of a job, in the interest of increased efficiency, what would happen to such men? Management has said: We will see that they have a job.
In any event, attrition will take its toll of the 200 or 300 men. Really the difference of opinion involves the definition of a longshoreman as opposed to someone who works periodically, either at the week end or in the evening, moonlighting in the labour market. A distinction exists, and must be resolved.
On the other hand, and here I do not speak on behalf, or with the authority of the Department of Labour, my sympathy lies with the longshoreman who, when struggling to work 500 or 600 hours, which is not very much by our standards-
Would the hon. member permit a question? Am I to understand from his last remarks that the longshoremen's union, in the three ports involved, permits moonlighting on the job?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: I know the hon. member who has asked the question is a labour man. You can define it any way you like. One of the paradoxes and hypocrisies of the labour movement is the willingness on the part of its members to fight each other, or anybody else, over certain aspects of labour; and yet, after a man has worked for 40 hours in one industry, he can stop working in that industry, and go somewhere else to work as scab labour. That happens all the time.

Does the constitution of the longshoremen's union permit a man to go to another union and moonlight?

June 1, 1966
Supply-Labour

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
These questions would be fine if we were in a standing committee. It is obvious the hon. member is not familiar with the practice in the Montreal area. Thousands of part-time workers are required in the Montreal area to help when times are busy. The point being discussed between management and labour is this: Into which category do these particular workers fall? Are they genuine longshoremen, or people who earn their living as watchmen, trainmen, railway-men or postal workers, and who go down to work on the docks during periods of peak activity?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
The difference of opinion arises because management is trying to define a longshoreman on the basis of the number of hours he works. I think this is wrong. A longshoreman who presently works only 500 or 600 hours a year may have worked 3,000 hours a year a few years ago when he had the vigour to do so. It may be his health has been ruined by his employment-by the almost inhuman working conditions to which he has been subjected. I do not think we should say, dietatorially, that because a man worked only 200 hours in a particular year he should not be entitled to job security. To do so would be cruel and inhuman; it would be in conflict with the Freedman principle.
Since there are comparatively few people affected, some four or five hundred, I suggest it might even be necessary to prepare a case history of each of these men. It might well be found that a man who had worked only 500 hours in the year just ended had worked on the waterfront for 20 years and should certainly be considered as a legitimate longshoreman.
These are some of the problems which representatives of labour and management are discussing today in Montreal under the guidance of an experienced mediator, Judge Lippe. subtopic: SUGGESTION TO COMPLETE NAVIGABLE WATERWAY IN WESTERN CANADA
SUGGESTION TO COMPLETE NAVIGABLE WATERWAY IN WESTERN CANADA
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of establishing an inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton, via the Red River, Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I first placed this motion, which requests the government to give consideration to the advisability of establishing an inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton, via the Red River, Lake Winnipeg and the Saskatchewan River, on the order paper in March, 1962. Each year subsequently I placed this private members' motion on the order paper, but was never lucky in the draw and the motion never reached the floor of the house for discussion. Naturally I am happy that it has now been called and an opportunity given to members to discuss it.
I was first prompted to introduce this motion by the promotional efforts of the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce who have been advancing this project for some years. The late Mr. J. F. (Fergie) Cunningham, who resided at Selkirk, Manitoba, was employed with the federal government's public works department and was in charge of dredging operations for the federal government in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and the Northwest
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]

Territories, was actually the author of the project. Mr. Cunningham had done a lot of research work on this proposed project. He had outlined it to members of the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce. I likewise had many personal discussions with Mr. Cunningham about it.
Subsequently the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce took over the promotional work for the project. They sponsored resolutions at the annual convention of the Manitoba Chambers of Commerce and at the annual meeting of the Hudson Bay Route Association, advocating an inland waterway in western Canada.
The Selkirk Chamber of Commerce prepared a brochure for a western inland waterway, which they subsequently distributed to members of the Manitoba legislature, members of the Saskatchewan legislature, members of the Alberta legislature, to all the chambers of commerce in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to all the daily and weekly papers in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, to the radio stations, T.V. stations, and to others. In 1962 I distributed this brochure to all members of parliament and all senators on behalf of the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce. The Selkirk Chamber of Commerce and I received many acknowledgements and some very interesting comments.
The purpose of the proposed waterway is to provide another means of transportation. It is natural that those who are already engaged in transportation will be opposed to it, and may even endeavour to ridicule the proposal. I believe that this western inland waterway will reduce freight costs from the prairie provinces, will accelerate development in northern areas, and will encourage production of minerals, as well as agricultural and forest products. It will open new frontiers to recreation and will encourage tourists to come to these areas. It no doubt will bring in much needed American dollars. In addition to this, it will shorten the distance for building roads to resources and will create substantial additional employment.
There are those who say that our population at present is too small for this type of project to be feasible. They say that when our population reaches 50 million this project will be both desirable and feasible. The population of Canada has now reached a total of 20 million people. From now on it will increase at a much faster rate than hitherto, and it will not be very many years until the population reaches the 50 million mark.
June 1, 1966
Where will this extensive growth take place? I believe it is a foregone conclusion that a lot of the growth will take place in the three prairie provinces. This is a natural area for industry to move to, and a western inland waterway will help bring about this expansion.
In the period from 1870 to 1917 the following boats travelled the Saskatchewan river system:	the Northwest, the Marquis, the
Northcote, the City of Edmonton, the Alberta, the Baroness, the Medicine Hat, the Manitoba, the Alberta, the Nipawin, the Strathcona, the City of Prince Albert, the Saskatchewan, the Lilly, the Commissioner, the Cumberland, the C. R. Smith, the Assiniboine, the Omega, the La Fleur, the Minnow, the Minasin, the Le Pas, the Notin, the Klondyke, the John Bull, the Archibald, the Sam Briskin, the Dispatch, the Emma E and The Pas. These boats ranged in length from 43 feet to 202 feet and travelled the river system without any expenditure for river improvement. Since some of them were 202 feet long they were not small boats, and they managed to travel the river system for all those years without any improvement being made to it.
An extensive detailed investigation to ascertain the feasibility and cost of providing a navigable waterway for vessels and barges from Edmonton to Lake Winnipeg was made between June, 1910 and October, 1915. The report of this investigation was submitted complete in November, 1917 by the chief engineer of the dominion public works department.
This report, based upon a minimum of six feet of water at mean low water levels from lake Winnipeg to Edmonton, estimated the cost as follows: dredging and channel improvement, $6,200,000; seven locks and dams, $14,565,591; for a total of $20,765,591.
When this report was received world war I was in progress. Then came the post-war years, and subsequently the second world war, but still no action was taken on the report. In those years, and up to recent times, the prairie region was mainly a grain economy, but now western Canada is becoming industrialized and this industrial development will grow at a rapid pace. It is therefore essential to have competitive transportation systems which will be able to provide low-cost transportation services. In my opinion a multi-transportation service will be needed to serve the needs of the people, and this will include truck, rail, air and waterways.
Navigable Waterway in Western Canada (5:10 p.m.)
Following the second world war, tremendous developments of waterways have taken place in the United States, in Europe, and in other parts of the world. The St. Lawrence seaway was built after world war II which now permits ocean liners to sail from Fort William and Port Arthur. In the United States the Mississippi river system has been developed into an inland waterway; the Missouri river is now an inland waterway. Another tremendous development is the Ohio river navigation system of 981 miles, with 53 locks and dams. Towns along these waterways have increased in size and have prospered.
Travel on inland waterways in Belgium, the Federal Republic of Germany, France, the Netherlands, the U.S.S.R. and other countries has increased considerably since the end of the second world war. Recently, new inland waterways have been developed in Italy, Germany, France, the U.S.S.R., Luxemburg, and so on. The Moselle waterway, a 170 mile link between the steel producers of Lorraine and the Rhine, was officially opened in the spring of 1963. The construction of the waterway was an engineering feat of some note and the cost was shared by three countries^-France, West Germany and Luxembourg.
This inland waterway enabled the French steelmakers to ship steel to prospective customers in southern Germany more cheaply than before. It also enabled them to bring in coal by barge from the Ruhr area and the Dutch ports and this means lower freight rates. This inland waterway is helping the economies of the three participating countries.
The proposed inland waterway from Winnipeg through Selkirk to Edmonton is approximately 1,200 miles. We are not talking in terms of seaway similar to the St. Lawrence seaway. The inland waterway which we are proposing would be suitable for tugs and barges.

This equipment moved a large volume of material and equipment during the construction of the Grand Rapids hydro power development. Speaking in the House of Commons on February 19, 1962, page 1031 of Hansard. I said the following:
Mr. Speaker, I have in my hand a copy of the Selkirk Enterprise dated March 8, 1961. The heading on page 3 is "Cunningham Visualizes Edmonton to Selkirk Water Highway."
Mr. Cunningham is a resident of Selkirk, Manitoba, and until his recent retirement was in charge of all dredging operations for the federal government in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories.
Mr. Cunningham, when speaking to the Selkirk chamber of commerce, outlined his plan for a water highway from Edmonton on the Saskatchewan river to Grand Rapids, down lake Winnipeg and up the Red river to Selkirk and Winnipeg. It was evident that Mr. Cunningham was talking about a subject with which he is familiar, and also that he has carried out a great deal of research work on this topic. It is also a topic in which he believes, and he feels it would be practical to make it a reality.
Whenever new ideas are advanced there are some who immediately say that those ideas are ridiculous and nonsensical and that the man responsible for them is a day dreamer. I am sure that when the St. Lawrence seaway was suggested

there were those who said the project was nonsense. After the idea had been advanced it no doubt took a long time to stir up interest in it and to convince people of the possibilities. Later, extensive surveys were required to determine whether the project would be of sufficient benefit to warrant the spending of public money. I have no quarrel with that. I do think it is important that this type of project be given careful study. I agree one has to be convinced of the over-all benefit to the country as a whole before public moneys are spent. I merely point this out because I am sure that throughout history whenever a progressive idea has been advanced there were those who referred to it as absurd. However, one should remember that the man advancing the idea has given study to the topic while those who criticize have usually not given the matter any thought or consideration, which is why they offer the kind of criticism I have mentioned. I am one of those who believe that whenever someone suggests a project, particularly when that project is imaginative and visionary, one should look at it carefully and give it every consideration.
The suggested program of Mr. Cunningham is one which. I believe, comes in that category. It certainly is imaginative; likewise, it is visionary. One can visualize this type of project leading to the development of the northern ports of the three prairie provinces. It is essential that we should provide all practical forms of transportation. Since Canada is a growing nation with an expanding economy and the likelihood of a greatly increased population in the years to come, I think it will be desirable to have varied forms of transportation so as to serve Canadians wherever possible. The presence of rail, freight, truck transportation, air lines and water transportation would tend to establish competitive freight rates which could not help but be beneficial to people in general.
I still hold the views which I expressed on that occasion and firmly believe that the time has come for the government to explore the cost and the feasibility of such a waterway.
I want to read one of the letters I received after distributing the brochure prepared by the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce. It is from the minister of public works of that time, and is as follows:
I was very interested in the brochure enclosed with your letter of March 15, 1962, describing a waterway between Winnipeg, Selkirk and Edmonton. Mr. J. F. Cunningham, the author, was an employee of the department for many years until his retirement a year or so ago.
The improvement of the various waterways of Canada is of continuing interest to myself and the members of the department. I have watched with interest the increasing use of such rivers as the Mississippi, Missouri and Ohio rivers of the United States and the rivers of Europe, where barge traffic has become a very important element in the national transportation system.
There appears to be two main requirements for an economic use of river waterways; these are, a large population and a mature industrial development. I am certain that in the future the area which would be served by the proposed Winnipeg-Selkirk-Edmonton waterway will have a large increase in population with many industrial centres.
June 1, 1966

When this has come to pass, I am sure that the vision of the Selkirk Chamber of Commerce and the people of the west will have become a reality.
In this letter Mr. Walker refers to two main requirements for an economic use of river waterways-a large population and a mature industrial development. We are gradually approaching both these requirements. We can dream a little further and again, looking into the past, we will realize that Selkirk and Winnipeg need not be the eastern terminal of this inland waterway. With channels of 100 to 150 feet wide having a mean depth of six to eight feet, large loads can be taken clear from lake Winnipeg to the Great Lakes via the routes of the old explorers, up the Winnipeg river Lake of the Woods system to the Great Lakes.
One can dream a little beyond even that and envisage the day when a seaway will also be built down the Nelson river to connect Hudson bay and Lake Winnipeg. Then western Canada would be connected by a seaway to the Atlantic ocean and Hudson bay.
