I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Stefanson) for his patience and his determination in bringing this motion forward after waiting three years. It is a dream which may well come to pass within this century. The suggestion of an inland waterway from Winnipeg though Selkirk to Edmonton is not a new one. In fact it is an old idea which has been discussed and studied for a number of years. An engineering survey of this project was first made by the Department of Public Works more that half a century ago, during the years 1910 to 1914, as pointed out by the hon. member who introduced the motion. Then the first great war broke out and the scheme was abandoned for the duration of the war. Other things happened to curb the enthusiasm of those few who favoured the idea at that time.
However, the idea has persisted. The interesting scheme to pipe water across the prairies to the cities of Moose Jaw and Regina, which had been suggested by Professor Hind of the University of Toronto in the 1870's would have meant the construction of a dam and a diversion at the Elbow river. The possibility was envisaged of travelling by boat all the way from Winnipeg to Calgary. This proposal by Professor Hind was knocked out by the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Then, there was the plan of Mr. John R. MacNicol, a member of parliament. His plan was to make the old fur trade route navigable for coal and oil transport which the hon. member for Selkirk seems to be advocating. In 1961 the premier of Manitoba requested a review of the information obtained in the survey made before 1914. The former minister of northern affairs and national resources also became interested in reviving the possibilities of the scheme.
This time the review concerned the engineering and economic problems associated with the canalization of the Saskatchewan
June 1. 1966

river, was restricted, as was the original study, to a determination of the justification for a detailed engineering study including a field investigation, preliminary design and cost estimates. The conclusion reached in 1961 was that there would not be sufficient volume of traffic to provide significant transportation savings to set against the heavy capital and operational costs which would be involved for the federal government in the construction of such a waterway. The assessment showed, moreover, that road and rail transportation systems now in existence would appear to be capable of meeting foreseeable future requirements.
It must be remembered that the transportation facilities in the prairie provinces are vastly improved now over the facilities available in the early days of this century when this project was first suggested. Then, the railways and waterways were the main transportation systems. Now, the Trans-Canada highway provides a direct first class route for interprovincial truck and passenger traffic and our air lines offer speedy passenger, freight and air express service between all major points.
Although the 1910-1914 engineering survey was confined to the route from Edmonton to Winnipeg and did not investigate the potential of the South Saskatchewan for navigation, it is still considered adequate for determining the order of magnitude of the costs involved in developing either or both the north and south branches of the Saskatchewan river for navigation purposes.
At this point I had hoped, if time permitted, to quote from a reliable publication a summary of the potential and weaknesses of the Saskatchewan river, as it was at the time the survey was made and as it existed until recently prior to the advent of the building of the Saskatchewan dam. I think a recital of the history of this famous river's behaviour is useful for the purpose of our discussion which concerns, of course, whether or not such a scheme as envisioned in this motion is economically practical. Thus it can be seen that this proposal, if judged by the standards set for the original engineering study, appears to be reasonable for the probable barge traffic that might be expected to use the river today. These provide for a channel depth of six feet and a width of 150 feet. The original study estimated the costs of providing navigation facilities from Edmonton to Lake Winnipeg at approximately $20 million. Using the quantities and designs of the early study 23033-371

It is extremely doubtful that present circumstances would result in a substantial downward revision of these costs.
One estimate made by a non-federal agency of costs for providing navigation facilities for lake Winnipeg to Empress on the South Saskatchewan river exceeded $250 million. This latter estimate, in the opinion of the engineers of the Department of Public Works, is excessive. It might be noted that one estimate is for a navigation route using the North Saskatchewan, and the other is for a navigation route using the South Saskatchewan. However, the review carried out in 1961 for the previous Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources found that it was reasonable to assume that a minimum cost of developing a navigation route originating on either the North or South Saskatchewan river and ending at lake Winnipeg would be in the neighbourhood of $100 million, and could possibly cost $250 million.
It follows that if the expenditure of $100 million cannot be justified on the basis of potential transportation savings, further study at the present time is not warranted. Let us look at the economic factors. The range of capital costs has been estimated to run from $100 million to $250 million. In the lower figure if amortized on a 50 year basis, the equivalent annual costs, including interest and amortization, would be some $5,500,000. On the higher figure, the annual costs would be $13,750,000.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. As I intimated, on the higher figure, the annual costs would be $13,750,000. Neither of these amounts include maintenance for operating expenses.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
The physical capacity of the locks in the proposed system was estimated at nine million tons of freight annually, on the assumption of equal traffic in both directions. However, it would be possible to handle only 4.5 million tons one way, and it would be highly improbable that the locks would be in continuous operation. Therefore a more realistic estimate of the capacity of the system would be in the order of 3 million tons a year.
It appears that by far the greatest volume of traffic that would move on such a waterway would be bulk cargoes such as coal, petroleum products and grain. These would be the only ones having any possibility of economic movement on the waterway during the estimated seven-month season. As I said before presumably the main movement would be from west to east, with little apparent backhaul traffic in sight.
In connection with the movement of coal by barge along the proposed waterway, the Manitoba Hydro-Electric Power Board has estimated that in 10 to 20 years, the coal requirements for its Selkirk plant will average 1 million tons annually. This is assuming that natural gas would not provide a cheaper B.T.U. base-an assumption that is open to question. As to grain and petroleum products there is nothing to indicate at the present time that the proposed water system would be competitive' with present rail rates for eastward movement.
Summing up, on the basis of these preliminary studies there would appear to be little justification for expenditures on works of the order of $100 million to $250 million in the interests of navigation on the Saskatchewan river. Hence it would seem doubtful that there is any reason to quarrel with the 1961 finding, which was that a large outlay on engineering investigations is probably not warranted at this time. If it is considered desirable some day to pursue the matter further it is believed that studies should be made first of all on the economic side and involve a more detailed analysis of traffic potential.
It may sound unpleasant to have to be realistic and dash cold water on such a
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Rinfret).]

romantic suggestion as a waterway through the heart of our great prairies. It would be much more pleasant to be able to agree with Professor Edward Kuiper of the University of Manitoba who, in a paper prepared for the 1961 Resources for Tomorrow conference said that a similar development would turn Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta into "the Garden of Eden of North America". Dr. Kuiper was of course referring not only to a waterway but to a full irrigation system that could be developed with it. Such a system, he said, would mean the end of drought for all time in the prairie provinces.
Dr. Kuiper's proposals were more ambitious than those of the hon. member for Selkirk. He also suggested the canalization of the Nelson river in northern Manitoba. Such a development, he said, would make it possible some day for Winnipeg residents to travel by boat deep into the heart of Alberta and, for a change, come back by a different route-through the Saskatchewan wheat fields to Hudson bay. He thought it would be a simple matter from a technical viewpoint to build ship locks in conjunction with future dams on the Saskatchewan and Nelson rivers.
However, the results of the preliminary investigations I have described to you indicate, I believe, that although it may be simple from a technical viewpoint, the capital expenditures involved would be very considerable, while the economic justification has not been firmly established in any of the investigations that have been carried out to date. In other words, there is little evidence to indicate that the results of the review carried out by the previous government in 1961 do not still apply.
Nevertheless, great changes have taken place in the prairie provinces in recent years in industrial and natural resources development, as well as in transportation. And in view of this growth and development, I would not want to suggest that the Win-nipeg-Edmonton waterway will not be built some day, nor for that matter that even Dr. Kuiper's more extensive proposals will, in the light of future development of the west, prove to be impossible. I trust, none the less, that this is a dream that the hon. member for Selkirk will see come true in the end.
